references.text: Jesus teaches the disciples about humility in service: Even after doing all that is commanded, they should call themselves "unworthy servants" who have only done their duty.

[ref:Job 22:2-3|Job 22:2-3] asks whether a human can be of benefit to God and whether the deeds of the righteous hold any value for the Almighty. This illuminates the thought in Luke 17:10 that even our best service does not put God in our debt.

[ref:Job 35:7-8|Job 35:7-8] emphasizes that human righteousness adds nothing to God—your righteousness concerns a human like you. This corresponds with the idea that servants are "unworthy" because God is not dependent on their deeds.

[ref:Ps 16:2-3|Psalms 16:2-3] expresses that our goodness does not reach up to God. David confesses that the Lord is his master and that his good deeds cannot add anything to God—a parallel to the humility Jesus requires in Luke 17:10.

[ref:Isa 64:5-6|Isaiah 64:5-6] describes how all human righteousness is like filthy rags. This recognition of our own inadequacy before God is the background for Jesus' words that servants should regard themselves as unworthy.

[ref:1 Cor 9:16-17|1 Corinthians 9:16-17]—Paul says he has nothing to boast about in preaching the gospel, for it is a necessity laid upon him; it is a stewardship entrusted to him. This reflects the thought in Luke 17:10 that one only does what they are obligated to do.

[ref:Phm 1:11|Philemon 1:11] uses the word ἄχρηστος/εὔχρηστος (unworthy/useful) regarding Onesimus. The root ἀχρεῖος (unworthy) in Luke 17:10 shares this conceptual world concerning a servant's usefulness or lack thereof.
[ref:Rom 3:12|Romans 3:12] quotes Psalm 14 and says there is no one who does good, not even one—and uses a form of ἀχρεῖος (unworthy). This underscores human inadequacy before God, as in Luke 17:10.

[ref:Rom 11:35-36|Romans 11:35-36] asks who has first given anything to God so that he should repay it. All is from him, through him, and to him. This idea that no one can put God in their debt is central to Luke 17:10.

[ref:Lk 12:37|Luke 12:37] presents the surprising image of the master himself serving his servants—an expression of God's grace that goes beyond duty. This contrasts with and complements the picture in Luke 17:10.

[ref:Mt 25:21|Matthew 25:21] shows that the master still praises the faithful servant and invites him into his joy, even though the servant has only done his duty. This reveals the dimension of grace that complements Luke 17:10.
